newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada agency okays AT&T Canada as carrier.
newsitem.headline: Canada agency okays AT&T Canada as carrier.

text.p: Canada's telecommunications watchdog said on Wednesday it has determined that AT&T Canada is controlled by Canadians and is therefore eligible to operate as a common carrier in Canada.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission said the structure of AT&T Canada, formerly Unitel Communications Co, as well as various safeguards ensure that non-Canadians do not control the company.
The CRTC said its decision is based on a review begun in December 1995 when Unitel launched a series of restructuring transactions.
These deals led to a new ownership structure for Unitel. It is now held by the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Toronto-Dominion Bank, the Royal Bank of Canada and a unit of AT&T Corp.
Canadians hold 66 percent of the voting shares.

The CRTC said eight of nine board members are Canadian. AT&T holds 33 percent of the voting equity and has a right to appoint three of the nine directors. The remainder are appointed by the banks or are independent. The independent directors cannot have any relationships or characteristics that could compromise their independence.
The board has overall supervision of the company's affairs, makes the major strategy and appointment decisions, oversees management, and has overall responsibility for company operations operations.
The CRTC said it believes that the structure, composition and powers of the board, and the role of the independent directors, ensure that the company is controlled by the board and not AT&T Corp.
But the CRTC has asked AT&T Canada to modify certain corporate agreements in order to guarantee the board will have an unfettered right to appoint all senior managers.

The CRTC is also ordering AT&T Canada to place on the public record numerous agreements and documents which formed the basis of the Commission's determination and for which the company had claimed confidential treatment.

Under Canadian law, facilities-based telecommunications carriers are forbidden from being controlled by non-Canadians, and sets a maximum level of foreign ownership at 20 percent of voting shares in the operating carrier and 33 percent in its holding company.
